case.title: Coursework in the age of chatbots at Lowmere School
case.question: How should Lowmere School keep coursework honest now that pupils can get a chatbot to write it?
case.story: Lowmere School (made up) has 900 pupils. Coursework counts for a fifth of several GCSE and A-level grades, and most of it is written at home. Teachers say they can no longer tell which essays pupils wrote themselves. Last summer, two pupils were caught and lost a whole subject. The head has £18,000 a year in spare budget and two free teacher periods a week per department. Parents are split between trusting pupils and wanting every essay checked.

in_the_news.headline: Ofqual: Using AI for coursework risks 'life-altering' penalties
in_the_news.why: Ofqual has warned that undeclared AI use in coursework can cost a pupil a whole GCSE or A level, and wants coursework better supervised; Lowmere has to decide what that means for its pupils.

facts.text: In England there were 100 proven cases of AI-related plagiarism in GCSE, AS and A-level qualifications in summer 2025, up from 85 the year before.
Of more than 4,500 teachers surveyed for Ofqual, 83% said unsupervised written coursework should have greater supervision or other controls.

sources.title: Ofqual: Using AI for coursework risks 'life-altering' penalties

tests.text: Names who checks pupils' coursework, how often, and a start date this school year
Gives a total yearly cost at or under £18,000 and says what it pays for
Lets a pupil who is doubted show their own work, with a named teacher to talk to, before any penalty
No pupil is penalised on an AI-detector score alone
No pupil without a laptop or a quiet place at home ends up worse off
Says how Lowmere will know, by next summer, whether cheating has gone down

voices.who: a shop worker, 50s, with a daughter in Year 11
voices.text: My girl works hard at the kitchen table. I do not want her marked down because a machine says it smells like a robot.
Do the writing in school where everyone can see it. Then nobody has to guess.
Fine, but name who does it and when. I have heard promises before.

voices.who: a care worker, 20s, left school at 16
voices.text: Half my class had no laptop at home. Make sure they are not the ones who pay for it.
The school has 18,000 pounds. Spend it on teachers' time, not on gadgets.

bench.angle: Supervised writing in class plus a short talk about it
bench.title: Write in class, then talk it through with a teacher
bench.answer:
What changes: from 5 January 2027, every coursework essay is drafted in supervised lessons. Each department uses its two free teacher periods a week to run these sessions and hold a five-minute talk with each pupil about their work.

Who: each head of department checks their own subject's pupils.

Cost: £16,500 a year: £12,000 for two quiet-room supervisors after school, £4,500 for 15 school laptops for pupils with none at home.

Doubt: a pupil whose talk does not match gets a second talk with their named teacher, Ms Reid, and can show notes and drafts before any penalty. No detector score is ever used.

Check: in July 2027 we count proven cases against last summer's two.

bench.angle: Buy a tool that scores every essay for AI use
bench.title: Buy a detector, scan every essay, treat the score as a clue
bench.answer:
Buy one AI-detection tool, about £6,000 a year, and scan every coursework essay. The head of school runs it from January. Essays with a high score go to the subject teacher, who reads them again. The other £12,000 stays unspent.

Detectors guess. They can flag honest pupils and are easy to dodge. So a score is only a reason to look, never proof. A flagged pupil meets their head of department and explains the work before any penalty.

Pupils without laptops are not affected, because the tool only reads handed-in work. By next summer we count flagged essays and confirmed cases against last year's two. If most flags prove wrong, we drop the tool.

bench.angle: Ban all computers for coursework and go back to exams
bench.title: Write coursework by hand, in school, with no computers
bench.answer: Lowmere stops home writing. From January, all coursework is handwritten in school, in timetabled supervised sessions. No computers. Each head of department runs it, using their two free periods a week. The head spends £16,000 a year on paid invigilators and exam-hall cover, and £2,000 on paper and folders. Nobody needs a laptop or a quiet room at home. If a teacher doubts a piece, the pupil explains it to a named teacher, the head of year, before any penalty. No detector scores are used. Next summer we count proven cheating cases and compare with last summer's two. Honest limit: exam boards set what coursework counts, so we cannot drop it ourselves, and some subjects need computers.

gate.verdict: A and C pass every test, with C exactly at the £18,000 ceiling. B passes five tests but is unclear on the no-laptop limit, since it dismisses the issue without saying how those pupils are protected.

jury.question: The school's plan has pupils write coursework in supervised sessions. Should every pupil do this, or only pupils whose work is doubted?
options: Every pupil, so nobody is singled out
Only pupils whose work is doubted
Every pupil can choose: supervised sessions, or hand-in work plus a longer talk
jury.ruling: Every pupil writes in supervised sessions, 8 to 3 with 1 for choice.

reasons.text: No child should be marked out as a suspect. Same rule for all.
Watching everyone for the sake of a few is too much. Step in where there is doubt.
Some pupils cannot stay after school. Let them choose another way.

minister.text: Lowmere adopts Answer A: coursework drafted in supervised lessons from 5 January 2027, a five-minute talk with each pupil, and a second talk with a named teacher before any penalty. £16,500 a year.
minister.statement: This answer passed all six of the citizens' tests, including both red lines: no detector score is ever used, and pupils with no laptop get a school one. It costs £16,500 of the £18,000. The jury ruled 8 to 3 that every pupil writes in the sessions, so no child is singled out. I want to know in July whether cheating has gone down. If it has not, we change it.
